Mr. Speaker, I cannot answer for the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce as to the preparation or the current status of that particular report. I know that a good deal of work has been done on it. Incidentally, I do not believe it necessarily needs to be a matter of argument. I return to the fundamental point. There is a question of how this can be dealt with in a manner fair to those who are dealing with countries which have boycott clauses, but which have not themselves done anything that is improper or in any way regarded by this House or by Canada as being an offensive type of action.
I suspect if the hon. members wish to have a reasonable discussion on how this matter can be dealt with, and at the same time indicate our abhorrence of the kinds of boycotts which all of us on this side and members opposite have always referred, then there is no good reason that we should not talk about it in a reasonable way. When the report is completed, I appreciate it should be dealt with, and we should carry through on our commitment. The matter is not a matter of saying how many have complied or otherwise with the boycott, or how many have been asked to comply. Strictly, it is a matter of finding out which companies have no reason to be reprimanded publicly and perhaps misunderstood publicly.
Hon. members opposite have claimed that we should not be doing anything which will make it difficult for companies to expand their export operations and the like or, in fact, to hurt their business within the country.

In my supplementary question to the minister I should like to ask him, in view of the revelations of the Carswell-Slaughter investigation of breaches of air safety regulations in northwestern Ontario, an example of irregularities by the national airline which was brought to the minister's attention by the National Dispatchers' Association, as well MOT investigation into the 1976 crash of an Air West airplane in British Columbia which concluded that the carrier did not meet safety standards and that Transport Canada's monitoring of the carrier's operations was inadequate, whether the minister will now admit that the situation is serious enough to warrant a full public inquiry into air safety regulations and their application across Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board
subtopic: ALLEGATION NAVIGATION ORDERS DISOBEYED-GOVERNMENT POSITION-REQUEST FOR PUBLIC INQUIRY
speechtext:
No, Mr. Speaker. The fact of the matter is that the investigation had revealed certain deficiencies which should have been corrected and steps have been taken to correct them. Obviously, there will be breaches of regulations, including air navigation orders by some individual operators. I would not want to join the hon. member in making it sound as though air carriers flagrantly abused the regulations, and I would even want to emphasize that it is completely untrue and unfair to carriers to suggest that they are frequently engaged in activities which are unsafe. The fact of the matter is that our standards in our air navigation orders are very high. That is the standard we want observed, but a breach of the air navigation orders in those circumstances may not always involve a high risk but only a failure to attain our very high standards. We still attempt to observe them and we are amending our air navigation orders where required to do so. We are appointing additional inspectors and we are following other recommendations which were made by our investigators who did a very thorough job.

subsubtopic: ALLEGED REFLECTION ON UNITED STATES AMBASSADOR ENDERS-REQUEST FOR CLARIFICATION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I wish to ask the Prime Minister a question concerning the ambassador of the United States, Mr. Enders, whose professional stature is reflected in the fact that having been appointed ambassador to Canada under a Republican administration he was retained by the Carter Democratic administration. On Wednesday the Prime Minister said that the Minister of Agriculture was speaking for the government when he complained about certain viewpoints expressed by the ambassador in speeches in Canada. This statement by the Prime Minister, if allowed to stand, will unfortunately diminish-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: ALLEGED REFLECTION ON UNITED STATES AMBASSADOR ENDERS-REQUEST FOR CLARIFICATION
speechtext: Order, please.

subsubtopic: ALLEGED REFLECTION ON UNITED STATES AMBASSADOR ENDERS-REQUEST FOR CLARIFICATION
speechtext: Did the Prime Minister intend to diminish the usefulness of Mr. Enders? I would ask the Prime Minister to clarify this most important matter.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subsubtopic: ALLEGED REFLECTION ON UNITED STATES AMBASSADOR ENDERS-REQUEST FOR CLARIFICATION
speechtext: Gladly, Mr. Speaker. I think I made it quite clear by my answer to the supplementary question that I consider Mr. Enders is free to state publicly in Canada the views that represent those of his government just as I would want our ambassadors abroad to express their views. I think Mr. Enders has been doing it consistently, and there has never been any complaint officially or any note sent to Washington from this government. I added that a minister is perfectly free to disagree, just as any other member of this House would be free to disagree with Mr. Enders. I had not and I still have not read the speech of the Minister of Agriculture. He may have used language which is colourful and which he frequently uses in this House. I am standing by the position that the Minister of Agriculture is free to criticize and disagree with Mr. Enders, but that Mr. Enders was perfectly entitled to speak for his government and to continue to do so.

subsubtopic: ALLEGED REFLECTION ON UNITED STATES AMBASSADOR ENDERS-REQUEST FOR CLARIFICATION

subsubtopic: ALLEGED REFLECTION ON UNITED STATES AMBASSADOR ENDERS-REQUEST FOR CLARIFICATION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would be surprised if the opposition agreed with the right of anybody to disagree with an ambassador who is speaking for his country. The interests of Canada are not necessarily those of the United States.

subsubtopic: ALLEGED REFLECTION ON UNITED STATES AMBASSADOR ENDERS-REQUEST FOR CLARIFICATION
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLEGED REFLECTION ON UNITED STATES AMBASSADOR ENDERS-REQUEST FOR CLARIFICATION
speechtext: There is certainly no intention to cast a cloud over Mr. Enders' capabilities or his ability to speak for his government. I do not think that is their job; they are there to represent the countries from which they come, not the countries to which they go. I respect Mr. Enders for taking the positions he does if they are those of his government. I just do not think we should be shy or embarrassed about disagreeing with him.

subsubtopic: MR. STEVENS-STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE RESPECTING BILL C-l 1
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege of which I have given you notice. It arises from what was said in the House yesterday by the Minister of Finance in response to a question put to him by myself with respect to the introduction of an important tax credit bill which has been proposed.
The minister stated, as reported at page 1893 of Hansard:
When we started Bill C-l 1 the hon. member said that second reading was to be three or four days and it lasted three weeks. Thus, I cannot rely on him very much.
I interjected that this statement was not true.

subsubtopic: MR. STEVENS-STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE RESPECTING BILL C-l 1
speechtext: It is true. You are unreliable.

subsubtopic: MR. STEVENS-STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE RESPECTING BILL C-l 1
speechtext:
I maintain that the minister, in making that statement, imputed bad faith on my part. He was suggesting I had entered into some kind of understanding or agreement with him with respect to the early passage of Bill C-l 1 through second reading. I deny that, without qualification. There is no truth in the minister's statement. There was no conversation between him and myself with respect to the time we might take on second reading debate of Bill C-ll.
Not only do I deny the truth of what the minister said, but I would draw to your attention a second untruth which I believe Your Honour can check for yourself by reading Hansard. The minister stated that Bill C-ll took three weeks at second reading stage. That is not true. Second reading began on November 7 and ended on November 24. If it had taken three weeks, the terminal date would have been November 28. So on the face of it the minister's statement is untrue. Further, I recall that not only did we spend a relatively short period debating Bill C-ll on second reading, but between the dates mentioned we had at least two supply days, and there were several questions of privilege raised-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: MR. STEVENS-STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE RESPECTING BILL C-l 1
speechtext:
Order. The hon. member is now expressing disagreement with the minister with regard to the duration of a debate on second reading. His question of privilege basically relates to a statement by the minister that there had been some consultation between him and the hon. gentleman about the second reading debate lasting three or four days.
I have to tell the hon. member that, aside from the fact that essentially we are dealing here with a disagreement, the remark complained of was made during the course of the question period yesterday. Our practice normally requires that any member wishing to raise such a matter by way of a question of privilege must do so at the earliest opportunity. The hon. member was here yesterday and the occasion for raising the matter as a question of privilege, had he wished to do so, was yesterday at the conclusion of the question period- not 24 hours later.

During today's question period the hon. member for Grenville-Carle-ton I think may have inadvertently misled the House when he indicated that an agreement had been reached in relation to the motion put forward by the member for Peace River, and that the Prime Minister had not been aware of that agreement. whether there was a disposition to limit debate or to have no debate at all on a motion to refer the matter, but no conclusion was reached. speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: These are the difficulties we face continually if we attempt to negotiate something on the floor of the House. Again it is an indication that we ought to firm up such arrangements before attempting to report them to the House or to deal with them on the basis of consent. I understand, however, that on orders of the day there may be some accord resulting from developments in the meantime, and we can deal with that at that time.

Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege. My question of privilege arises from the statement that you have just made. I feel that you have put me in an unbelievably untenable position. I was attempting-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Order, please. I want to remind the hon. member, I hope for the last time, that whether or not the hon. member seeks to agree or disagree with rulings by the Chair, rulings by the Chair on procedural matters are final. 1 have made a disposition in respect to the procedural correctness of the hon. member's position. As the hon. member said in his remarks today, he complained yesterday from his seat, at the time the remark was made, that the remark was not true. The hon. member was in his seat, he was aware of the remark, and he said that it was not true.
I do not often lean on the requirement that a matter of this sort be raised on the first occasion. I have often extended leniency in that regard. However, if the rule is to be respected at all, certainly in a situation where the hon. member recognizes a remark to the extent of denying it from his seat in the House, as he did yesterday, he must surely recognize that, if there is any validity at all to the regulation, I have to enforce it in these circumstances. I do not take particular pleasure in that. That is the primary concern.
In any case, on balance there is a direct disagreement in this matter. The hon. member has put his accusation and his denial of what the minister said yesterday on the record and has said it is untrue. He has done so under the guise of a question of privilege. It is not a question of privilege, but in any case, even if it were, the only time it could have been properly raised in the procedural sense was yesterday.

subtopic: PROPOSED REFERENCE TO COMMITTEE OF GREEN PAPER ON FREEDOM OF ACCESS-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank hon. members on both sides of the House for their accommodation, and I also offer thanks for the alacrity with which the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) has accepted the invitation to have a debate. 1 am only sorry that the Prime Minister is not here to debate the matter, because he has learned a lot about security and ministerial responsibility over the last few weeks. He has had a very "Liberal" education with respect to this matter, and I had hoped that he would be here for this debate. However, I see my hon. friend, the Secretary of State (Mr. Roberts) is here, and I have reason to believe that in general he believes in good legislation, at least to the extent that cabinet solidarity permits him.
The period of gestation for any reform is always fairly lengthy, though with this government it is extremely lengthy. Hopefully, because of the number of conditions which have been placed on this reform, we are getting close to the stage of reaching committee and we may be able to do something constructive on this very important issue concerning circumstances in this country and other countries in the civilized and democratic world.
I believe it was John Stuart Mill who mentioned the necessity of there being a free marketplace of ideas in order for there to be good government. A free marketplace of ideas does not exist where you have government secrecy. Government secrecy has been the way of life of many governments in democratic countries. 1 hope we are now coming to a stage where that will be concluded. Government secrecy is a palpable defect. It is widespread. It has run so deep that it has become a malignant disease and what I would call a political distemper which constitutes a major impediment to the free marketplace of

December 16, 1977
Access to Documents
ideas. It spawns corruption, incompetence and indecision. We have seen a lot of that, Mr. Speaker, over the last two or three years.
It is a major factor in the cynicism and loss of confidence which has spread over this land. Any member of this parliament who is honest will agree with me when I say, travel any place in Canada and you discover a feeling of outrage, frustration, anger and disbelief among the people which has constituted an impediment in the capacity of governments today to deal with the problems which afflict us. Most of those problems are man-made and can be cured by man. It takes a relationship between the government and the governors which is non-existent not only in the federal system of which I have some knowledge but in other systems of government in this country.
Mr. Speaker, people may forgive politicians and governments for erring, but they will no longer forgive them for lying, for deception, for procrastination linked to deception which have become the trademarks of Ottawa. Open government by a workable freedom of information law will have very definite advantages for this parliament and for the public of Canada. Canadians are entitled to know what the government is doing to or for them, what it is costing them, and who will receive the benefits of the proposals which are made. This parliament will then be a better place. We will have a more efficient question period, with crisper, shorter questions, if members of parliament on both sides of the House are armed with the knowledge permitting them to contribute to any debate in a meaningful, effective way.
The right of freedom of speech is often talked about. Mr. Speaker, what good, what use and what value is freedom of speech without the knowledge upon which we can base that speech? I am convinced the quality of debate in this House will be vastly improved when and if that time comes. The word is "when" because this has become a major issue. I do not believe the public will tolerate refusal by this or any other government, be it federal or provincial, to delay the enactment of a workable freedom of information law. When it comes, Mr. Speaker, it will be a better parliament because of the quality of the speeches we will be making and the questions we will be asking.
There have been challenges to the kind of law which most of us want and when I say "most of us", I give credit to a great many people on the government side. If I were free, under our rules, to introduce a freedom of information law myself, and should it be put to the question without any whips being present, 75 per cent of the members of this House would support it, and at least that percentage in the other place. We would then have a bill in short order.
The government is indicating that they have approached this problem with undue caution, with Scots caution, delaying caution. They talk about ministerial responsibility. Mr. Speaker, ministerial responsibility in Canada has become a farce, a myth. It no longer exists. The average minister does not know one per cent of the work being done in his department. He is, in effect, the spokesman, the advocate for his department and

its officials. He reads the departmental brief in cabinet, in cabinet committees, to this House and to the public.
By the very nature of the kind and quality of our government, the massive intervention the government has made in the lives of people, it is impossible for any minister to know what is going on. Even when he is given information by senior civil servants on how his particular department is run, he comes into this House and what is the situation? We had a typical example during the last few months, specifically in the past few weeks, regarding security. By interpretations which have been placed by the Chair based on precedents of this House- and I do not challenge them-we have been prohibited from questioning ministers who have considerable knowledge, or should have, of the workings of the Department of the Solicitor General. These people are eminent parliamentarians-I will use that expression as it is Christmas time. However, under the Government Reorganization Act, the Prime Minister is able to move a minister to another department when things become awkward, and he falls outside the scope and scrutiny of this House. That is the situation which exists. How can you have ministerial responsibility in a situation of that kind?
The situation is of ministers sent to a royal commission under terms of reference established by the Prime Minister, by personnel appointed by the Prime Minister who will report to the Prime Minister. This royal commission may hold many of its deliberations in secret. How can that be held to be, in any sense of the imagination, ministerial responsibility? Anyone who suggests ministerial responsibility constitutes a barrier to a freedom of information act should have been in this House for the last two months. They would then know it does not constitute any meaningful alibi.
We talk about ministers having the right, the final word, and not the judges. Every day of the year, magistrates in the federal and provincial courts examine issues dealing with federal and provincial legislation which involve making a judicial interpretation of certain aspects of government behaviour initiated by ministers. We have many examples. The Solicitor General (Mr. Fox) has shown no unwillingness to seek judicial guidance on certain decisions he has arrived at in the course of the debate on security. Four times he has seen fit to go to a judge, and each time he has been rejected. For a government which states that it is not prepared to entrust to judges the right to scrutinize the decisions of ministers, the Solicitor General shows a remarkable alacrity to accept another attitude.
We have the case of the Minister of State for Urban Affairs (Mr. Ouellet) who went to a judge with respect to an issue. We have the case where the AIB program was referred by this government to the Supreme Court of Canada. During the days of the year when courts are sitting, they have occasion to decide and deal with issues in which the government is involved. I say to you, Mr. Speaker, that is not a reason. The real reason is-and we all know it; members on the other side know it; cabinet knows it-fear of exposure, fear of embarrass-
December 16, 1977

ment. Those are very understandable fears for a government which has been in power for any length of time.
The reasons advanced by this government are precisely the same as those advanced by President Nixon, through his counsel, to the Supreme Court of the United States. Also, these reasons were advanced on behalf of the Harold Wilson cabinet in the United Kingdom when the court was considering the Crossman diary litigation which exposed the workings of the United Kingdom cabinet for what they were. It is the fear of embarrassment and the fear of being caught-not viciously or in terms of corruption, but it is human nature not to want to be proved wrong. I am sure ministers of the government make as many mistakes as myself, and perhaps more. There is no reason why their mistakes should not be exposed and subjected to scrutiny by this parliament, on behalf of Canadians. This does not constitute any barrier to the passage of legislation.
Today, the hon. Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Gillespie), acting through a whim of secrecy, evaded a reasonable question posed by the hon. member for Saskatoon-Biggar (Mr. Hnatyshyn). My colleague was asking for information about the uranium cartel. Members of this House, and Canadians generally, are entitled to that information. The period is long past when that information would be of any consequence. It is a terrible thing for members of the public to witness the manner in which the minister evaded a proper question put by a member of my party.
In conclusion, we are not seeking something which will put this country or the government down the drain. Any government can live with it. We want a declaration indicating that all documents in the possession of the government are available for examination by the public and by parliament, subject to certain precise exceptions. There is little disagreement between the government and members of my party as to what the exceptions will be: they can be thrashed out.
As soon as possible, we would like to see indexing of documents to enable members to identify them. It is a humiliating and demeaning experience for members of the opposition to be required to rely on leaks from public servants in order to perform their duties. We are entitled to something better than that. We must have a proper appeal process to an independent tribunal. The decisions of that tribunal must be binding on the government and the other party concerned. I would like to see rules making that procedure simple and inexpensive, so there is no delay. People should be allowed to obtain a document on the payment of a reasonable fee. I do not think it should be free: the fee would pay for the cost of the service.
If the government believes there is no public support for this suggestion, it is wrong. We have gathered support from 45 or 46 organizations which have a total membership of approximately three million people. These organizations are of some substance and are influential. I will not get freedom of information by leading an attack on the barricade; but if the
Access to Documents
government delays implementing a proper, workable, freedom of information law prior to the next election, it will have a penalty to pay and its name in the history books of this country will be lower than it is at the present time.

subtopic: PROPOSED REFERENCE TO COMMITTEE OF GREEN PAPER ON FREEDOM OF ACCESS-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first I should like to congratulate the members of parliament who participated in this most excellent study. I did not have an opportunity to participate, but the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Brewin) did on behalf of the New Democratic Party. This is a substantial move toward finally having a meaningful bill presented in this House.
I endorse what was said by the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin). He indicated that it was incumbent upon this government to do something once the study comes out of committee. The reason for that, and the reason we are now hearing a few cooing noises from the government side concerning this subject, is that the government now realizes the political impact of this particular subject. Canadians are tired of seeing a government which represents a bureaucracy rather than its constituents. That is the key question in terms of freedom of information. The lockup between the government and the bureaucracy should never be so close that the difference cannot be recognized.
The House has witnessed a substantial amount of evidence concerning the Royal Canadian Mounted Policy inquiry, as well as many other matters, where ministers have failed to distinguish between the interests of their own bureaucracy and the interests of the public. Often there is a distinct conflict between those two areas.
I congratulate the hon. member for Peace River for doing an excellent job by bringing this matter forward once again. In an untiring way he has led the fight to bring forward a decent piece of freedom of information legislation.

subtopic: PROPOSED REFERENCE TO COMMITTEE OF GREEN PAPER ON FREEDOM OF ACCESS-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: PROPOSED REFERENCE TO COMMITTEE OF GREEN PAPER ON FREEDOM OF ACCESS-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
We should not forget the contributions of other members in the House. I am thinking particularly of Barry Mather who sat in this chamber as a member of the New Democratic Party for many years. From 1965 to 1970, yearly he introduced a private members' freedom of information bill. Also, I would not want to discount the efforts of the hon. member for Greenwood or those of the venerable and honourable member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) who has been an untiring advocate of freedom of information in this House.
From time to time we receive interesting answers on the subject of freedom of information. When one requests the opening up of bureaucracy to provide more information to the public, quite often a minister of the government will say, "All you are doing is increasing the cost of government, the volume of work, the number of employees, the number of computers, as well as duplicating work".
Approximately a year ago I went to Washington to look at their freedom of information law to see whether there was any validity in the answers which I was receiving from the

December 16, 1977
Access to Documents
bureaucracy and the ministers. Possibly the environmental protection agency was hit hardest by the United States freedom of information legislation, and their people totally support that legislation. The result in the United States is that a person simply writes a letter requesting information. There is a time limit for the agency to reply to that letter. The request does not have to be fulfilled if the information provided is not specific enough. The person is required to pay a nominal charge for duplication, and the information is forwarded.
Our government has forgotten that these documents are not the property of the government, nor members of parliament; they are the property of the public who pay the taxes, and they are entitled to that information. The sooner that fundamental principle is realized, the sooner Canada will have a freedom of information law.
I was delighted with the recommendation suggesting the establishment of a panel of judges to review the question. It will wash the dirty linen of the RCMP. If one looks at the wiretap legislation, he will see the same principle is involved. When the government decided on the wiretap legislation, they decided we would allow judges to issue warrants on wiretaps except in matters of national security. We do not have confidence in the bench for that; we will let the Solicitor General do it. Again, that is a fundamental weakness.
I say, trust the courts, trust the judges. With the capacity they have and the tenure they have, they are the best we can have in the country to protect the civil rights and freedoms of Canadians. On many occasions this government has felt it could not invest the courts with that kind of trust. I hope that the all-party report will also spur the government forward in those areas-sometimes, of necessity, in camera-in providing the courts with the decision-making process in those areas.
We will probably see a bill. I am afraid I am cynical enough to believe it has something to do with the timing of the next election, but 1 urge the minister seriously to consider these recommendations, particularly in terms of narrowing the definition of information which may not be released, and particularly with regard to allowing a panel of judges to make the final decision. There is no way that a minister can act objectively on a request for information which may be embarrassing to his personal performance. The old cliche that justice must not only be done but must be seen to be done never applied more than it does on the question of freedom of information.
I do not want to be long-winded. I just want to say how delighted our party is that this report has come forward, and how delighted we are that members of parliament such as the hon. member for Ottawa West (Mr. Francis) are associated with it and have placed their names on it. We also have our Social Credit friends associated with the report. I hope that the efforts which have been made by many members of the House will now come to fruition.

subtopic: PROPOSED REFERENCE TO COMMITTEE OF GREEN PAPER ON FREEDOM OF ACCESS-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would also like to give my support to the motion, which has been expected for some time and should lead to a statute ensuring greater freedom of information. Such freedom of information has been requested by everyone, not only by members in this House. Because when members ask for information or the production of certain documents, when they insert questions on the order paper, very often it is because of queries from their constituents.
And when, as very often happens, we are told we cannot have the information because it is confidential, we wonder whether we are not dealing with some kind of in camera government. A democratic country such as we have in Canada is entitled to something better. Sometimes we are told that questions on the Order paper cannot be answered because this would be too costly, too expensive in terms of both time and money.
Mr. Speaker, if a question is too expensive in terms of time, in terms of research to find answers, it may be that there are deficiencies on the part of the bureaucracy, that bureaucrats do not take the trouble to keep note or maintain files of their actions and expenditures. If such files were kept up to date, it would be easy to give us the required information without too much time or money.
Mr. Speaker, I therefore feel that members of parliament and the general public need to be better informed if this Parliament is going to perform its function in a democratic country.
In my view, the bill that has been called for by the opposition and a variety of organizations working in that area should bring more freedom of information without putting the government in hot water, which too often is what they fear.
Mr. Speaker, in very limited areas only should the government withhold information, but as I said, in a democratic government information must be readily available, to meet the Canadian people's information needs.

subtopic: PROPOSED REFERENCE TO COMMITTEE OF GREEN PAPER ON FREEDOM OF ACCESS-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to say, first of all, that I welcome this initiative on the part of the honourable and learned gentleman. It helps me meet the commitment which 1 made to the House and to him, that as quickly as possible we would have the government's green paper on access to public documents forwarded to the joint committee. As hon. members know, we have had on the order paper a government motion to that effect. I welcome his motion, just as I welcome the activity of the joint committee in studying this extremely important issue. I welcome, as well, the initiative of my friend, the hon. member for Ottawa West (Mr. Francis), and the members of the committee of which he is chairman.
Some hon. [Members: Hear, hear!

subtopic: PROPOSED REFERENCE TO COMMITTEE OF GREEN PAPER ON FREEDOM OF ACCESS-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
I think that their contribution is extremely useful to the discussion of this important question, and I know

December 16, 1977

that the joint committee will be looking at their recommendations. I want to add that it is my hope that other organizations, such as the Canadian Bar Association and others, will come forward to the committee with constructive suggestions on how we can improve the position which has been outlined in the green paper on access to public documents.
I want to say, also, that it is not a question of whether there is great public support for these changes which I think all members of the House wish to make. The hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin) assures me that there is great public support for these measures. I would say to him that even if there were not, these changes should take place because they are essential to the functioning of a healthy democratic society.
At the outset of his remarks, the hon. member for Peace River asked me to specify, within the balance of the possibilities of collective responsibility, my commitment to the principle of open government. I am pleased to do that and to draw his attention and that of members of the House to the first two paragraphs of the introduction to the green paper on legislation on public access to government documents. Having written them myself, they represent my sincere view and also the commitment of the government to follow the precept of open government.
It has always seemed to me a paradox that in the parliamentary system-with its emphasis, at least in the past, upon confidentiality within the public service, and secrecy of decision-making in the cabinet and secrecy of party decision-making in various caucuses of the various parties-that in a country which espouses open government, so much of the decision-making process should take place behind closed doors and away from public view.
The commitment, which has been eloquently expressed by the hon. member for Peace River, is one which members on the government side share and, indeed, one which is shared by members of all parties.
I can say parenthetically-I do not think the hon. member will mind-that his view that one of the results of the legislation would be to improve the quality of the question period is something that I would devoutly support. Anything that would improve the quality of the question period or that would assist in the improvement of the kind of questions put by members of the opposition is a step devoutly to be wished for.

Access to Documents
The hon. member cited John Stuart Mill, a Liberal for whom I have a particular affection. I think the hon. member and I would both agree-if I can return a quotation of Mill's to supplement his own-that, "Whoever knew truth to be put to flight in a fair encounter?" It is my commitment-and I think it is evident in the paper that it is also the commitment of the government-to ensure that as much information as possible is available to the public and to hon. members, so that a full understanding of the context of decision-making is available and so that the public can properly judge the efficiency and the correctness of decisions which are taken.
In the few moments that are left to me, I want to emphasize the purpose of the government's presentation of the green paper on legislation on public access to government documents. I am sure hon. members of the House appreciate, but members of the public may sometimes not, that the green paper is not a description or a setting forth of policy positions to which the government is committed in a hard and fast way. It is, rather, a study document. It is a document prepared for the purposes of examination and discussion, and that is the process we have followed in presenting the green paper.
Some have interpreted the green paper to be-and they are mistaken in their interpretation-a disguised hard and fast policy position, and they feel that the various options which are described in the green paper are not really options but are a kind of stalking horse for some policy which has already been decided and which will be unveiled in a hard and fast way at a certain time. I want to emphasize that that is not the case.
The government is presenting this study paper because it genuinely thinks it is important to move in this area. We think there are problems involved, and we very much wish to have the counsel of the joint committee on the recommendations made in the paper. We are not committed to either the specific exemptions which we have described nor to any specific review process. We are committed to the idea of implementing open government in this country and expanding access to public documents. We accept that material prepared at taxpayers' expense should be available for the public to see unless there are extremely good reasons why it should not be so available.
I want to draw the attention of the House to pages 10 and 11 of the green paper which outline in a tentative way a possible description of what exemptions there should be to the basic principle of providing access, which we accept. I do not argue that the description of these exemptions is perfect in the document we have presented. There are many difficult problems to wrestle with. Some have suggested that we should, for instance, simply apply the standards or the language used in the American freedom of information act, but because we have a different system of government, the effect of applying the words used in that act might be unforeseen. There might be undesirable effects which hon. members of the opposition-not me-would be the first to resist. We have presented the American wording and we have also presented the wording which was used in Australia in relation to some of the exemptions, to try to get the committee to focus on this question and

December 16, 1977
Access to Documents
to assist us in coming up with better wording if better wording can be found.
I want also to refer to pages 16 and 17 of the green paper which outline the review process and present five options or five different approaches. There may be others. If there are others, I hope the committee will present to us other ways of reviewing how the exemptions might be applied in practice. Here, too, we see that there are problems. The fact that the green paper discusses those problems should not be taken as an indication that the government has settled upon one final approach as to how a review process should be undertaken. That is not the case. We are open and willing to consider the recommendations which will be made to us by the committee.
There are problems with judicial review. There are problems with many of the options described. Judicial review can often be a costly process. Perhaps it need not be so. Perhaps there are ways of achieving the objective which I believe hon. members on both sides wish to achieve without the process of judicial review. That is one of the matters I hope the committee will look into very seriously.
Questions of ministerial responsibility are important. As the hon. member for Peace River has indicated, over the past few weeks the House has been considerably exercised as to what the responsibilities of ministers are and how they should be enforced. I doubt that members of this House would wish to see us implement a policy which would tend to undermine the accountability of ministers to the House. However, again we throw those questions, which can be complicated questions, to the committee for discussion and we are eager to have the counsel of the committee and its advice on those questions.
The hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Leggatt)- who, unfortunately, is not now in the House-referred to the question of cost and the experience in the Elnited States. I would like to point out to hon. members that on pages 26 and 27 of the green paper the whole question of cost is discussed. Apart from the whole process of judicial review, the estimated present cost in the United States of administering their freedom of information act is, in round figures, approximately $150 million a year. I would not for a moment suggest that because the process is costly, it should not be embarked upon; but I think hon. members will want to know what the cost will be for whichever of the various approaches to the question may be taken.
As hon. members will have noticed, I am not in very fine voice today. I do not wish to go on at great length. 1 hope the committee will wish to have me come and speak to it: I am anxious to do that. I believe that for technical reasons it is important for me to move an amendment. I, therefore, move:
That the motion be amended by changing the period at the end thereof to a semicolon and by adding the following words:
"and that a message be sent to the Senate to acquaint Their Honours thereof'.
The hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin) says he is always anxious to consider improvements to his motions. I hope he agrees that this change is an improvement.

I believe it is incumbent upon me also to ask for unanimous consent to withdraw my motion No. 8 which had as its purpose to do what the hon. member's motion does. The hon. member's motion seeks to refer the green paper to the joint committee. That is a commitment we have made. Mr. Speaker, I do not want to delay this debate. I certainly do not want to interfere with the right of any member to intervene at this moment. I would simply say, in summation on third reading, that we as a government have adopted a very flexible stance in relation to this bill, in a genuine attempt to try to accommodate the disposition of all members. Perhaps this is the reason we had some difficulties at report stage in trying to achieve that objective. However, I followed that flexible course in both committee stage and at report stage. We feel we have achieved a very broad basis of consensus on the elements contained in the amendments to this bill which reflect the disposition of members of parliament, the ad hoc committee, and largely, if not totally, the Chief Electoral Officer.
I would underscore one point which I think is more significant than any of the others. Allowance has been made in this bill, through the amendments at report stage, to accommodate the voting rights of those who are teachers and administrators attached to DND bases overseas. This is a very important step forward. A number of representations have been made by individual members and by the Teachers' Federation. We, as a government, are very pleased to associate ourselves with the achievement of that objective. It is an achievement and objective that can be shared by members on both sides of the House. We consider it a very important step forward.
The second point I would make is with regard to motion No. 15. Although it has not received unanimous consent, I would simply indicate, with regard to that motion dealing with the difficulties being experienced through a particular by-election, the problem being referred to generally as the Roach case, that the government never did strike a particular disposition. We attempted to respond to our perception of the disposition of members of the House of Commons in bringing forward an amendment that we felt would be acceptable. The fact that it did not receive unanimous consent does not in any particular way aggrieve the government in that regard. We were simply trying to serve what we perceived to be the interests of members of parliament.
I do not think it is necessary for me to recount all the amendments related to this bill: they are well known. I spoke

December 16, 1977
Canada Elections Act
of the original amendments and the nature of them at second reading. I addressed myself in very brief form to each of the amendments at report stage. In connection with the committee, the record stands for itself as to the disposition we have taken in that regard.
We think it is a positive step to come forward with these amendments. We hope they will substantially improve the application of the Canada Elections Act. I want to express, on behalf of the government, appreciation to the committee members and to the House of Commons for a tremendous degree of co-operative effort in order to help achieve a bill which affects each of us individually, all of us collectively, and all Canadians in general.

Mr. Speaker, I had not intended to rise on third reading of this bill, but in light of what has occurred I feel I must. I agree with the remarks the minister made a few moments ago. There has been a degree of co-operation and flexibility shown, not only by the minister and the government but by members of the committee and, in most instances, by members of all parties on the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections. It was a repetition of what has gone on in that committee since I became a member of parliament in June, 1968. I have been a member of that committee since the twenty-eighth parliament in 1968.
We spent almost two years dealing with the entire Canada Elections Act. Most of us on the committee also sat on a special committee on election expenses. We worked on that project for about a year and a half and then submitted a report to parliament on election expenses. We sat again when the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections dealt further with the Canada Elections Act and amendments thereto.
During those nine years and some months, outside of some good-natured teasing it is one committee where there has been a minimum of partisan politics and a maximum of co-operation, accommodation, compromise and mutual agreement. On one occasion, the major provisions of the Canada Elections Act changes were dealt with by committee of the whole. At that time, the same kind of non-partisan co-operation was evident. I recite all this because that is one committee where there must be a maximum of co-operation and a minimum of partisan political activity. That committee must deal with election law and election expenses. On occasion there are references to that committee dealing with members' rights and privileges. Therefore, there must be a minimum of partisan politics and a maximum of co-operation and flexibility in order that we may, as often as possible, arrive at unanimity in our decisions and reports to parliament.
In many instances, the amendments to Bill C-5 to amend the Canada Elections Act were agreed to in committee, with only the very rare occasion where there was a vote or division. Amendments by government members and members of opposition parties were accepted. It is very rare in parliamentary committees that the government and the responsible minister are as co-operative and flexible as they were on this occasion.
[Mr. Cafik.J

Whatever one might think of the deputy government House leader, he is a nice fellow personally, but he is also a very tough politician, and partisan in terms of his political beliefs. But even he set an example by way of co-operation and flexibility by doing his utmost to meet the wishes expressed in favour of changes in Bill C-5. He returned to his cabinet colleagues and in most instances got approval for changes to be made, which meant that he, as the minister piloting the bill through the House, had to bring forward amendments and royal recommendations at the report stage. I believe that in every case this was done at the request of members of this committee and of opposition parties. That is a good example of co-operation, a good example of all parties working together to get the best possible election provisions.

speechtext:
Perhaps not in every case, but certainly in most cases. I mention this because I feel badly that we could not have decided all the motions which had been accepted by the Chair or with which there had been unanimous consent to deal. Every member has the right to withhold unanimous consent, but I submit that if this right is not used with care and good judgment, it is being abused. On this occasion I feel the right has been abused; I feel it has not been used with care and good judgment. I say this in spite of my liking for the hon. member for Lanark-Renfrew-Carleton (Mr. Dick).
Motion No. 15, with which we could not proceed because unanimous consent was not given, embodies an amendment without which a loophole remains in the law allowing the spirit of the elections act to be subverted. In the committee, the hon. member talked a great deal about closing such loopholes. I sincerely believed that he would be the first among all the members of the committee to be concerned about ensuring that it would not be easy to evade or subvert the intent and spirit of the elections act. I heard him on frequent occasions express his fears about brown-bagging and the diversion of funds to areas in which they should not be used. Our failure to deal with motion 15 could mean that his fears would be realized. I cannot fathom the reason he would not want this motion dealt with.
I believe it was understood that on this issue, as well as on several others, we would give unanimous consent as necessary when we reached the report stage, on the basis that these were measures which needed to be taken. They concerned matters which have been fully discussed in the committee on privileges and elections. On May 15 they were discussed by an ad hoc committee comprised of senior representatives of all the parties meeting with the Chief Electoral Officer, and that committee reached the conclusion that amendments must be made to the bill with respect to third party advertising.
It seemed to me that the degree of co-operation and agreement expressed then was being fulfilled by the government and by the minister through the presentation of motion 15. We liked the motion as far as it went, though had we been given an opportunity to discuss it, I would have gone further by moving
December 16, 1977

an amendment to strengthen it. But even had my amendment failed, the motion would still have meant the strengthening of the legislation.
The argument put forward by the hon. member for Lanark-Renfrew-Carleton yesterday in justification of his desire not to deal with this motion was that the matter was presently before the courts. I am not a lawyer, Mr. Speaker, but the hon. member is, and he should know a lot more about such matters than I do. But the precedent for passing or amending legislation in this parliament and in other legislatures while matters are before the courts has been established on a thousand occasions. I need only remind hon. members that when we were enacting amendments to the Criminal Code in 1969 and 1970, hundreds of cases involving the Code were before the courts directly relating to dozens of the sections we were amending. If the hon. member's argument were to stand, it would mean that parliament should not, and would not, deal with legislation at any time as long as the subject was somehow or other before the courts.
The hon. member's argument is so palpably absurd that I am surprised he would even put it forward. Parliament could not function if we were to follow his logic to a conclusion. Motion No. 15 and the amendment I would have moved would have been a valid exercise for the House to deal with. The hon. member's statement about the subject being before the courts is totally irrelevant. The hon. gentleman does not have the support of his own caucus with respect to the matter, and the House should be aware of it. His own party organization wanted this matter dealt with. In leaving this loophole open, we have provided a possibility that the intent and spirit of this law may be evaded.
I believe there is a deficiency in the law with respect to third party advertising. I say at the outset that in no way do I wish to infringe upon the freedom of speech or upon the right of every citizen to express his views before, during or after election campaigns. But the public has long demanded election laws and provisions to control election expenses so as to require that money spent by political parties is indeed spent on behalf of parties and candidates for office. It includes provision for disclosure of contributions in excess of S100. The law provides for controls on such expenditures, and that there shall be reimbursement for some portion of this expenditure by the national treasury. It also provides, but inadequately so, that if there is advertising carried on by those other than a political party, its official agent or candidate, which is of a political nature, it shall be construed as political advertising and the cost thereof must be shown.
The Roach case, as it is called, which is before the courts is an example of how the election law was weak in this area. It showed how a citizen, with the most honest and best intentions, may have broken the law. But the law is unclear. In my opinion, the Canada Elections Act is not clear enough, and frankly I do not think it is strict enough.
Canada Elections Act
I should have liked to see an addition to the law to include not only the motion with which the minister would have required unanimous consent to deal, but an amendment to the last part of the motion. So that the last paragraph would have read as follows:
-he did not mention or display the name of, or specifically identify,-
Then I would have inserted the following words:
-or did not explicitly or implicitly offer support for, or opposition to, any candidate or registered party.
I feel that the motion suggested by the minister, on the advice and at the request of the ad hoc committee composed of all political parties, with my amendment would have done what I believe we all want to see done. If even then it was still deficient, we would have had to wait until the courts decided, should the court be presented with a case to decide.
I said earlier that there is implicitly, in this kind of provision in our electoral law, that fine line between what would be evasion of the law and the freedom every citizen has, namely, the right to freedom of speech. It is perfectly proper and fitting for any individual, organization or association in our nation, during election time as well as any other time, if they so wish, to buy a radio spot, television ad or ad in a newspaper to expound their views on an issue of the day, and to call upon fellow citizens to support that view. That is a valid and worth-while exercise, whether or not any of us agree with that particular point of view.
However, where an individual, organization or association purchases a half-page or full-page advertisement in a newspaper, for example, in the midst of an election campaign expounding a certain view in support of any one of a dozen or so issues, whether capital punishment, marijuana, abortion, negotiations having to do with the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade, issues which are now or which will become current, and that individual, association or organization, not a political party or candidate or the agent of a party or candidate, specifically, explicitly or implicitly identifies a candidate or a party, or offers support for, or opposition to, a party or a candidate, then the advertisement becomes a political advertisement, the cost thereof should be assessed and the matter dealt with in accordance with the other provisions of our election law.
I am saddened that the hon. member for Lanark-Renfrew-Carleton (Mr. Dick) took the position that he did. If he wishes to oppose this kind of motion, he could well have done so. He is very capable on his feet and he could very well have done so in a debate on the motion or in a vote on the motion. I hope we are going to continue to have the degree of co-operation and non-partisanship that has been almost historic in the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections; but I say to my hon. friend that what he did today severely jeopardizes for the future what has gone on among members of parliament for many years.
Whether or not one likes a particular item which is proposed or is under discussion, this has always taken second place to the committee accomplishing the maximum amount of work,

December 16, 1977
Canada Elections Act
particularly in the area of election law and control of election expenses. This is something that is basic and fundamental to the welfare and good order, not only of our parties and candidates who run in elections but of the whole nation. I hope the hon. gentleman will decide that he can no longer be a member of that committee, that he no longer wants to sit on it. I want to tell the hon. member that there were many occasions when I did not want to be so co-operative; I wanted to raise hell and I had to bite my tongue and force myself not to. But that is a secondary consideration. We did not always get the kind of law and amendments that we wanted, but at least we had something that was common to members of all parties in the committee, and has been for the 9'/2 years I have been on the committee.
I am pleased with the improvements which have been made in the law by the rest of the amendments. I think they will generally prove to be of value and will make it easier for candidates and parties to abide by the law. A great deal of work will be required on the part of parties, candidates and workers to educate themselves and to inform the public of the provisions in this new law. I do not doubt for a moment that during the course of and following the next general election it will come to light that many mistakes have been made. Since the law is new, we will all be working under it for the first time. But I am convinced that the overwhelming majority of the mistakes will be honest ones.
There will have been no deliberate intent to evade or avoid the provisions of our law. No doubt there will be a few cases which the commissioner of election expenses will have to deal with. I would not be surprised to see a small number of official agents or candidates, or even elected members, paying some very severe penalties all the way from jail terms to losing the seat to which they have just been elected. That may well happen in a few instances. There will be some mistakes made, but they will not be deliberate mistakes. We will need that experience to learn how well the law operates.
The amendment we have passed to provide for review is particularly pleasing. Once all the returns are in and expenses are filed, the Chief Electoral Officer refers the reports to parliament. The privileges and elections committee can meet subsequent to the next general election and assess the experience, the results, how successful the limitations on expenses are, and if the reimbursement provisions meet the requirement. There are a host of other things we can review and make recommendations to parliament for any changes that may be necessary in a future parliament for preparation of a subsequent election. That is a valuable provision, Mr. Speaker, and I would like to see it in many other pieces of legislation. After a certain period of time has passed, there is a provision for review by a committee of this chamber.
I express my disappointment at not being able to deal with an important and fundamental point regarding third party advertising. I am pleased with the success we have had-some of it not as much as 1 and other members would have liked-in

dealing with the remaining amendments in this bill. I hope that by passing this bill today they will have provided the Chief Electoral Officer with sufficient time to get ready for a general election. I hope that we have made it easier for him and his officials to carry out the implementation and the overseeing of this law.
I wish to express the commendation I made to the minister and the members of the committee for their co-operation, and particularly to express appreciation and gratitude to the Chief Electoral Officer, Mr. Jean-Marc Hamel, and his staff for the many hours they spent during the day and at night meeting with members of our committee, with members of the ad hoc committee, and meeting in the office of the chairman of the committee, assisting us, providing information and answering questions. If it had not been for their co-operation, we would not be at the stage we are now.
I hope, Mr. Speaker, that the amendments we have made will prove beneficial to all Canadians.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, to begin with, we should mention the people in the ad hoc committee who contributed so much. Actually, they were the master craftsmen of this bill. They were instrumental in whatever improvements have been made to the bill. I am not saying it is a poor bill. We all received much co-operation. But to those unsung heroes who probably do not have the opportunity to express their views in such a forum as this, I particularly want to mention Mr. Hamel and his staff. Also, Mr. Laschinger who represented our party at the ad hoc committee. There are many others, whose names I do not know, who were very much in evidence representing other parties of the House of Commons.
I would like to congratulate the chairman of the committee, the hon. member for York East (Mr. Collenette), for his work in handling the committee. He did exceptionally well. It was a committee where there was much harmony and co-operation. I would also like to mention the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Reid) who took a very active and co-operative part in the proceedings. One of the amendments we brought in was indexing. At this time, when everyone is talking restraint, our party in particular felt it very necessary that we ask for an amendment to the indexing clause. After researching the last ten by-elections, on a party average only 89 per cent of the limit which would have been allowed under the act was spent. Taking these things into consideration, and coupled with the economy of the country, we could not go along with the indexing of pensions at this time. Probably in the future, after the next election, this could be reviewed. We are not saying the door has to remain closed forever. Taking everything into consideration, we reached the conclusion that we must oppose indexing at this time.
Mr. Speaker, concerning the anonymous donations, there were several recommendations presented to the committee. We felt at this time that was just a way of buying the election, so during the committee proceedings, from the beginning we objected to the brown-bagging, as it is called, and asked for all donations to be accounted for. That was another restraint that

December 16, 1977

was needed. We want to be responsible and know where our money is coming from, and to keep election expenses clear and above board.
I was disappointed a little while ago, after we had started debate on third reading, to hear so many members kill time on an issue which means very little now in terms of changing the legislation. We expect this bill will be passed, and I think too much time has been taken this afternoon criticizing this bill.
I hope the amendments that have been made will do much to strengthen our political system. I was also a little disappointed in motion No. 8, in that the government refused the amendment respecting cases where the returning officer and the poll clerk were of opposite political faith. The province of Ontario has seen fit to extend this provision to the opposition parties. In this modern day of politics, Mr. Speaker, it is only fair that the two parties, one party representing the government and the other party polling the highest votes, should have a choice in naming either of the two people involved in the polls on election day. I thought the spirit of co-operation that we enjoyed in the committee probably would have prevailed here. That was one motion that we tried in a small way in committee, but we were stonewalled. Voting is the absolute fundamental or bottom line of the democratic process, followed by who is allowed to vote, and the ease of access to vote. It is not simply to give a certain percentage of the population a vote; it should include all people within the system who are properly and democratically citizens of communities. After that, when universal suffrage is operative, all the people within the system should have equal access to the right to vote and it should be easy for them to exercise it.
In the last election during 1974, a particular situation arose in my riding. A lady who suffered a handicap registered her particular concern that she, and others like her, would be humiliated and would have some difficulty exercising their right to their franchise. As a result of that, at the beginning of the first session of the thirtieth parliament, I submitted Bill C-292, which would assist the handicapped by providing the minimum difficulty possible to them in order to exercise their vote.
I am pleased, as are other members who have private members' bills included, that the particulars of the bill were
Canada Elections Act moved on to committee. In turn, the committee and the Chief Electoral Officer did everything possible to accommodate us. The end result is that in my bill, clauses 29, 50, 51, 52 and 53 accommodate a particular problem. It is not a universal answer to the problem; it is a beginning. In urban areas, where someone has a handicap, is wheelchair-bound or suffers from some other type of infirmity, rather than facing the possibility of being carried into a polling booth or humiliated in some other way, they will have access to an advance poll. That level access will be advertised in notices of advance polls and, in turn, without too much difficulty people can transfer their votes to that advance poll.
In the future we will have to consider all people who want to play a full role in a true democracy, despite their particular situations or backgrounds. There should be better facilities for them in the future. Through the accommodation of the Chief Electoral Officer and the committee itself, my particular private member's bill has gone forward incorporated in Bill C-5. At least it is a beginning. Even if people are handicapped, they are every bit as good, as bright or as much a participant as anyone. Because these people have suffered handicaps and have survived as good Canadians, we should lean over backwards within our democratic process to prove to them that we want the particular understanding and sensitivity of their vote exercised. Therefore, I am proud that this has come forward and will be a part of this new act. I hope the Chief Electoral Officer and members of this House will consider the possibility of extending it on a much wider basis.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as we have been listening to this debate I am sure that all of us have been thinking how fortunate we are to live in a democracy where there is open access to the political process. Equally so I think the care and attention which members on all sides of the House have given to the details of this bill are evidence of how important it is, and how members prize access to the political process. The very careful attention, as a number of members have said, and the non-partisan quality of the attention given in committee are another indication of the importance of amendments to the Canada Elections Act.
The amendments that have been made in recent years have all been aimed at broadening the basis of participation. An amendment was made some time ago to allow new citizens earlier access to the political process. I want to address myself very briefly to the question of new parties.
There are two national parties now represented in the House which began as regional parties. Changing times require different responses. Political parties express the way in which people want to work for social betterment and social change. Different times require different solutions, and a statute which is aimed at some degree of permanence obviously must provide ease of access for new parties which may be needed in future times.
In this connection the hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre (Mr. Benjamin) yesterday described, very accurately I think, the tax credit as being the most progressive measure introduced since universal suffrage. But measures that are intended for the common good may be misused by a minority, and I think there is a potential for abuse through a loophole which exists in the present bill and which it was not possible to close now but which I hope the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections will address when it next considers amendments to the Canada Elections Act.
At present there are 15 fringe groups which have signified their intention to run candidates in the next election. If they meet the requirements for auditors, and so on, and if they nominate 50 candidates, they will maintain their rights until the following election, whenever that may be. Thus, regardless of their share of the popular vote, regardless of whether the public has indicated support for their policies or their ideas, as things stand, any fringe group which has 50 candidates nominated and which has met the other requirements will be able to retain its right to give tax receipts. I suggest that this is perhaps not the intention of the act and therefore should be reviewed.
Canada Elections Act
If I may make my point with figures, let me point out that of those 15 fringe groups which are now ready to organize candidates in the next election, two ran a substantial number of candidates in the last election; one party obtained nationally 16,260 votes, or .17 of the total votes cast, and the other party obtained 12,100 votes nationally, or .13 of the total votes cast. To put it another way, neither of these parties which claim to be national parties received as many votes as the one independent member who sits in the House.
While I think it is extremely important that access be kept open for new parties, I also suggest that in future, after having allowed a party access during one election, if at the end of that election the voters by their ballots give a message that a particular party is not accepted, as indicated by its share of the popular vote, consideration be given to de-registering that party.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do no intend to take up too much time in this third reading debate, but having sat on the committee in past months when we were preparing suggested amendments, and then having sat again as we studied the amendments brought forward by the government, I have a few things to say.
I am always a little concerned when all-party co-operation reaches the point where one finds a prairie radical praising the extent of that co-operation. Something has gone rather sadly wrong when that happens, and while I do not ordinarily consider myself an iconoclast, I become a little suspicious when I hear a hymm of praise being sung to cosy arrangements by which everything is worked out through a thoroughly mutual agreement. I am happy to say that there was an instant or two in the processing of these amendments when committee votes were held even if that meant that objections were overridden by a majority of people opposed to the objectors. However, at least that happened.
The essential system in Canada errs basically as long as we have a situation-and this is my personal opinion, not the party doctrine-where tax funds go to help finance candidates, and I hope that the review promised after the first real test of the Canada Elections Act will take a good look at that aspect.
When everybody concerned is involved with the central authority and is partially funded by it, we have a breeding ground for cynicism, particularly amongst the young and the disaffected. I was not in parliament when that major change in principle was accepted, so I do not feel personally responsible for it.
I am concerned-and I am glad the hon. member for Trinity (Miss Nicholson) raised this-about the weaknesses of the Canada Elections Act in terms of the frivolous party and the frivolous candidate. I know one can become very sanctimonious about democracy and easy access through this act for everybody, but one of the things about modern electioneering and modern technology is that both have vastly increased the rewards to people who are either neurotic or slightly

December 16, 1977
Canada Elections Act
deranged-and I hesitate to use those words-who manage to get over the easy hurdles to become candidates and who may have a sufficient number of like-minded friends to be registered as a national party. To me this is done with ridiculous ease. There are televised all-candidate forums, halls are rented, and other opportunities are provided.
There is an enormous amount of free publicity for anyone who manages to become a candidate in an election. There is a great capacity for mischief. We are so deeply into the process of funding mischief publicly at election time that 1 think we must examine this aspect very seriously.
Through the Canada Elections Act I suspect that we will have succeeded in producing ballots which will be of enormous length. The candidate field will become increasingly crowded by people who will have no particularly good reason for being there except a love of attention and lust for the free publicity which comes with the electoral process.
We have spent a lot of time on the issue of easy access to polling stations. Nobody would deny that there are benefits, whether they are for teachers overseas, the military, or the handicapped. All that is entirely and utterly praiseworthy, but we have still failed to adopt a permanent voters' list and a full scale absentee ballot. Until we do that I do not think we can be very proud of our easy access.
We have extended slightly the provision for advance polls. That takes care of the holiday week end trap into which we have fallen in recent elections. I am very concerned, however, about the clause which slipped through, over objection, regarding the extended eight days of voting in the returning officer's office. I am gravely concerned about control. I know how busy those offices are during the days prior to an election, and the last thing a returning officer wants is to have people showing up over a period of eight days asking to vote. I am not talking about advance poll dates.
Does this mean that the 15, 16, 20 or whatever number of registered political parties there might be will have scrutineers sitting around the returning officers' offices? If that is the case, they will be all over the place, and I suspect that the efficiency of the offices will be greatly hindered and that in the end, particularly in close elections-and I speak as one who has suffered through one of those-it is going to be dismaying to find, when everybody thinks the ballots are counted, the returning officer showing up with one more barrel collected in those eight days, dumping it out, and possibly altering the result of a close election. I will be interested in seeing how that little clause works in actual practice.
I know that when we speak of a permanent voters' list the question of the terrible expense is always raised, but I have yet to see a really good analysis of what that expense would be compared with the expense of our present enumeration system.
One of the things that amazes me in our increasingly urban society is the way the Canada Elections Act still reflects in several instances the old myth that country life is pure, serene, and innocent, and that city life is corrupt and defiled. I suspect it works both ways. In town two people do the enumerating,

but in the country there is only one. On the other hand, I suspect it is easier now to miss an entire high rise apartment block than a single farm house in a rural area.
There are many anomalies. A missed rural voter can be sworn, but not an urban one. I find this kind of discrepancy between urban and rural amazing, particularly when our urban population is so enormous in proportion. When we pass Canada Elections Act amendments I am surprised that there is not rioting in the streets of our larger urban centres. However, people do not seem to be quite aware of how much this myth, which has outlived its day, persists in this act. I still suspect, though, that the reason we never seriously face up to the question of a permanent voters' list is our delight as politicians in the enormous source of small patronage which is handed out very directly and individually at election time.
I hope within the next decade or two we can adopt a permanent voters' list that would permit a full-scale absentee ballot. It would be much better than scrapping the list after every election. That strikes me as a pretty amateurish move when through technology the election, campaigning, disclosure, use of the Income Tax Act and many other things have become very sophisticated. In this one area, however, we remain singularly primitive.
I am happy for the change that provides that the cost of a recount can be borne publicly if the margin is low enough. I know from personal experience how easy it is, when margins are small, to find a variety of ways in which minor factors can mean winning or losing an election. I fought one close election where an entire community was disenfranchised without recourse. I admit the circumstances were unusual, but they lost their vote until the next election four years later.
It seems that 1972 is the last year for which we have the report of individual expenses of those candidates who declared them. I could not locate one for 1974 and I think I know why. In the majority of cases in 1972 the winning candidate was the one who spent the most money. Where he spent about twice the amount spent by the other candidates, the majority was higher.
I was pleased to see that the move to index election spending has been halted. There are parties in this House who have some way to go to meet the limits which, to my mind, are ridiculously high. The escalation of election expenses has been fantastic. When I came here in 1965 I declared $2,160 in election expenses and was the second "cheapest" member elected that year in terms of expenses. In 1968 my campaign cost $6,000; by 1972 it was up to $12,000, and in 1974 it was $17,000. That kind of escalation of expenses is unnecessary, but even at that the $17,000 spent in 1974 was well below the limit set in the act.
I think many elections should pass before the limits are raised. In our deliberations here we have greatly contributed to the cost of elections. I would rather some of that money went to the development of a permanent voters' list and an absentee

ballot rather than toward an over-kill in election campaign expenses.
